rv.q: This is in every sense a work of art, as tough and weighty as it is fiercely beautiful.
Delivered with consummate composure by Rose, it has the force of ritual.

She’s enacting an attempt to smash the weighty legacy of the Atlantic slave trade. The gesture is cathartic — the block splinters dramatically — but the evidence of the past can never be annihilated. In part this is a travelogue, recounting Thompson’s efforts to retrace Britain’s slaving routes.

Yet as she steps out from behind a table, we see she is wearing thick, black boots. Katherine Radeva's design hints at the idea that although Salt. is a spiritual diasporic journey, this comes at the cost of the very real, grounded labour which comes with unpacking inherited trauma.
In Dawn Walton’s engrossing production, Rose is dressed in a symbolically white dress, and her performance is a warm mixture of passionate anger and intimate confessional.

cn.t: Critics praise this powerful one-woman show about the Atlantic slave trade's legacy, with Rochelle Rose wielding a sledgehammer to shatter rock salt in a cathartic exploration of historical trauma that's both painful and poetic.
